summary.oneLiner: Delhivery delivered a bellwether FY26 with >1B parcels shipped and a decisive pivot to free cash flow positivity (Rs 89 Cr) one year ahead of schedule, driven by record volumes in Express/PTL and a margin turnaround in Supply Chain. The core thesis shifts from growth-at-all-costs to capital-efficient scaling, with ROIC expanding to 16% and net working capital compressing to 11 days, validating the operating leverage of the integrated network.
summary.business: Delhivery runs a pan-India integrated logistics network spanning Express Parcel, Part Truckload, Supply Chain Services, Full Truckload, International and Local services, offering door-to-door parcel delivery, B2B freight, warehousing and fulfilment, cross-border shipping, intracity delivery and supply-chain software. Its customers are e-commerce marketplaces, direct-to-consumer brands, SMEs, consumer-to-consumer senders and enterprise shippers across FMCG, consumer durables, consumer electronics, lifestyle, retail, automotive and manufacturing, with value-added services such as forward and reverse logistics, cash-on-delivery management, payment collection and fraud detection. The model is asset-light: Delhivery invests in critical service elements, automation and IP-sensitive parts of the network while delivering much of the physical capacity through network partners and last-mile partner agents, all orchestrated by a self-developed logistics operating system.

Full Truckload: Freight Index One (FTL pricing intelligence platform)
International: Air-parcel service for SME and enterprise exports
Software: Supply chain software / logistics software as a service

currentContext.strengths: Integrated single network: Express Parcel and Part Truckload run on the same gateways, line-haul and sortation infrastructure, letting capacity be shared across business lines and giving PTL shippers e-commerce-like turnaround times on several lanes|Proprietary in-house logistics operating system with over 80 applications, plus configurable APIs and libraries that internal and external developers build on|Data intelligence and machine learning across geo-location, network design, route optimisation, load aggregation, ETA prediction, product identification and fraud detection, drawing on fifteen years of proprietary shipment and telemetry data|Automation scale: 47 fully and semi-automated sortation centres, 129 gateways and 10.4 million shipments/day rated automated sort capacity, with machine-vision guided truck loading and system-directed floor operations|Network reach and density: services in 18,830 PIN codes covering approximately 97% of India's deliverable addresses, 71,362 partner agents and 52K+ active customers|Asset-light model with no real-estate ownership and only part of the deployed fleet owned, using managed marketplaces to match partner capacity to demand — lower fixed cost and flexibility to seasonal swings|Scale leadership: largest third-party Express Parcel network by volume and second-largest player in Express PTL, reinforced by the Ecom Express integration which added density, route viability and lower marginal cost per incremental parcel|Experienced entrepreneurial team drawn from engineering, technology, operations, R&D and design across industries
currentContext.strategies: Grow share in the core Express Parcel and Part Truckload businesses by adding network volume, since higher volumes make more routes viable for faster and cost-efficient delivery and deepen the operating leverage of the integrated model|Use the completed Ecom Express integration to hold client volumes, densify coverage, improve route viability, speed up delivery and absorb additional volume at lower marginal cost|Build out new service lines — Delhivery Local (on-demand intracity), Delhivery Rapid (2-4 hour intra-city fulfilment) and Delhivery International — and keep investing behind them|Keep technology and engineering at the core: in-house logistics operating system, proprietary data intelligence, LLM and multimodal AI across voice, vision, location intelligence and real-time transaction processing, SOP2Code/Spec2Code pipelines and a purpose-built agentic harness, moving towards in-house AI maps and 'physical AI'|Continue operationalising and upgrading automated infrastructure — extending the work at the three mega-gateways (Tauru, Lonad, Hoskote) and inducting newer material-handling systems, high-speed sorters, AGVs and ASRS — explicitly to raise throughput and reduce exposure to wage inflation and labour availability constraints|Develop in-house software and integrated hardware for mobile robotics and truck loading/unloading automation through the R&D team set up in FY26, targeted at pallet movement and lower truck turnaround time|Invest in homegrown talent: convert contractual workers into permanent roles, promote from within, and expand training through the Delhivery Academy and the Skill Development Programme|Expand welfare and inclusion — the Abhayam benefits programme for the 1 lakh-plus frontline workforce, living wages, and more opportunities for women including all-women hubs|Run an asset-light model that invests in critical service elements and IP-sensitive parts of the network while delivering physical capacity through a large partner network operated as a managed marketplace
currentContext.expansion: Delhivery's capital expenditure is directed at fit-out infrastructure, state-of-the-art automation and IT assets, and tractor-trailers; automation covers parcel sorter systems, bag sortation systems and conveyance systems plus future-ready technologies such as automatic guided vehicles, automatic storage and retrieval systems and unmanned aerial vehicles. The company owns no real estate and only a portion of the fleet deployed in its network, so spend is deliberately concentrated on critical service elements and IP-sensitive parts of the network while physical capacity is delivered through partners. During FY26 it capitalised Rs 4,933.26 million of property, plant and equipment and intangible assets (excluding additions through acquisition and disposals), carried Rs 9.67 million of capital work in progress at year end, and funded the programme entirely through internal accruals and available cash; capex intensity fell from 5.2% of revenue in FY25 to 4.7% in FY26. The named FY26 projects were the expansion of mid-mile facilities in Chandigarh, Gurgaon, Ludhiana, Patna, Jaipur, Ahmedabad, Guwahati, Pune, Cochin, Lucknow, Goa, Purnia and Rudrapur, and the deployment of 123 additional 46ft tractors to raise the share of tractor-trailer capacity in the linehaul network. Automated material handling systems run at the Bhiwandi (Maharashtra), Tauru (Haryana) and Bengaluru (Karnataka) gateways, leaving 47 fully and semi-automated sortation centres, 129 gateways, 158 processing centres, 99 fulfilment centres (7.5 Mn sq ft of warehousing under management) and 4,848 last-mile distribution centres at 31 March 2026. On the inorganic side, Delhivery acquired 100.0% of Ecom Express, the #3 independent express player in India, for a consideration of about Rs 1,371 crore, aimed at cementing its position as the No. 1 independent express parcel player; one-time integration costs covered shutdown of redundant facilities, dismantling and transfer of automation equipment, exit from contracts and employee exits. Fleet and energy investment continued: 123 tractors added taking the tractor fleet to 624, 30 more LNG tractors taking that fleet to 50, over 3,000 contracted CNG- or electricity-powered vehicles in first-mile, carting and last-mile operations, and installed solar capacity of 5 MW at the end of FY26 which the company aims to augment during FY27. Liquidity to fund further organic and inorganic growth stood at Rs 45,553.32 million of cash and treasury investments against outstanding borrowings of Rs 25.35 million, with capital commitments (net of advances) of Rs 1,373.86 million contracted at 31 March 2026.
currentContext.mdna: Formalisation of India's logistics market: customers are consolidating supply-chain spend with integrated 3PLs that offer reliability, visibility and nationwide reach, which management says drove share gains across all service lines in FY26|Operating leverage compounding at scale — rising volumes plus a steadily improving cost structure from years of automation and network engineering investment, and added volume density post the Ecom Express integration; EBITDA margin moved from 1.6% in FY24 to 4.2% in FY25 to 6.1% in FY26|India macro: IMF puts India as the fastest-growing large economy with growth around 6.5% in 2025 and 2026, nominal GDP of Rs 351 trillion (US$4.1 trillion) in FY2026, inflation around 4.7% in 2026, and consumption-led growth with PFCE rising as a share of GDP|Market size and mix: total India logistics market of US$247-270 billion in FY25, with road transportation holding around 66% of cargo movement by tonnage; global logistics market growing at a 10.7% CAGR to US$18.23 trillion by 2030|Rising consumer incomes — GNI per capita compounding ~9.3% between FY2020-2025, high- and middle-income households up from ~174 million in FY2020 to ~218 million in FY2025 with ~55 Mn more projected by FY2030|Digital adoption: online shoppers projected to grow 8-10% CAGR from FY2025 to 365-430 million by FY2030, aided by cheap smartphones and among the lowest data costs globally|New B2C commerce models — social commerce, omnichannel, quick commerce and D2C — plus category expansion into consumer durables, home and furniture, increasing demand for reliable organised logistics|Evolving B2B models (direct-to-retail, direct-to-consumer) and government programmes like Make in India and PLI, driving demand for speed, precision and visibility in B2B supply chains|Post-GST demand for integrated warehousing, transportation and technology from a single provider rather than mono-line players, plus growth of Tier 2 and beyond favouring players with deep national capabilities|Technology-led transformation of the industry — automated sortation, AMRs, ASRS, wider WMS penetration, connected logistics/IoT and 5G, and AI in supply chain operations for large nationwide networks|Headwind acknowledged by management: a challenging macro backdrop at the end of FY26 from geopolitical tensions affecting crude oil prices, with FY27 starting with significant geopolitical risk

risks.risk: Fuel price volatility with imperfect pass-through
risks.note: Fuel is a major portion of transportation cost and diesel prices track imported crude. Management notes pass-through is handled through contractual fuel price adjustment mechanisms that may operate with a time lag, may have defined thresholds or caps, and may not fully offset sudden or sustained volatility.

risks.risk: Geopolitical shocks to crude oil supply
risks.note: Conflicts in the Middle East and disruption around transit routes such as the Strait of Hormuz have sharpened oil-price uncertainty; after the U.S.-Iran conflict broke out in February 2026 Brent rose over 60% from about US$72/bbl to a peak near US$118/bbl in March 2026 before moderating to about US$93/bbl by August 2026, feeding into Indian diesel and petrol prices in May 2026. Management also flags that FY27 has started with significant geopolitical risk.

Migration during harvesting and election periods creates delivery delays and higher dwell time at hubs, forcing idle-capacity overheads and premium costs for emergency temporary staff; reliance on a transient workforce is described as a structural risk to service-level agreements and long-term supply-chain stability.

Drivers find the profession unattractive because of weak security and safety, harsh conditions, irregular hours and long time away from families, constraining line-haul capacity even as road infrastructure and ADAS-type technology improve conditions.

risks.risk: Reverse logistics and return cost in e-commerce
risks.note: Customer returns create complexity around pick-up timing, communication with pick-up personnel and packaging, adding cost for sellers and weighing on the growth economics of e-commerce logistics.

Manpower availability, inadequate road infrastructure, traffic congestion, poor address mapping and weather disruptions cause delays, higher cost and lower customer satisfaction in the last mile, which matters most for e-commerce and FMCG shippers.

Numerous small players operating independently across supply-chain segments cause suboptimal resource utilisation, lack of standardisation and coordination difficulties — a structurally competitive, low-standardisation market that organised players must consolidate through technology platforms, logistics parks and hubs.

The Unified Labour Code implementation of November 2025 consolidates 29 labour laws into four codes, universalises minimum wages and extends social security to gig and platform workers; together with the September 2025 GST 'Next-Gen' two-slab reform and April 2026 CBIC courier-export reforms, the compliance and cost base of a large contractual and partner-agent workforce is exposed to statutory change.

one-line thesis: Delhivery delivered a bellwether FY26 with >1B parcels shipped and a decisive pivot to free cash flow positivity (Rs 89 Cr) one year ahead of schedule, driven by record volumes in Express/PTL and a margin turnaround in Supply Chain. The core thesis shifts from growth-at-all-costs to capital-efficient scaling, with ROIC expanding to 16% and net working capital compressing to 11 days, validating the operating leverage of the integrated network.
financial scorecard: Revenue: Rs 10,486 Cr (FY26), Rs 2,848 Cr (Q4); EBITDA: Rs 764 Cr (7.3% FY26), Adj. EBITDA margin 6.3% (Transport), 10.9% service EBITDA (SCS); PAT: Rs 347 Cr (FY26, 3.2% margin), Rs 87 Cr (Q4); Order Book: Healthy SCS pipeline with 2 new mandates activated in Q4; Net Debt: Net Cash position >Rs 4,500 Cr. One-offs: Integration expenses for Ecom Express factored in yet FCF remained positive; no major accounting distortions noted.
guidance: Revenue Growth: Express volume grew 72-73% YoY in Q4; Margin: Express targeting 16-18% normative range, PTL margins expanding sequentially; Order Inflow: SCS pipeline margin-accretive with strict hurdle rates; Capex: Intensity reduced to 4.7% of revenue, targeting ~4% going forward, unaffected by AI/robotics pilots.
order book & pipeline: SCS business turned profitable with Rs 79 Cr service EBITDA (4x YoY); 2 new mandates signed/activated in Q4; Pipeline described as 'healthy' and focused on consumer durables, auto, and lifestyle sectors with disciplined client selection.
segment / subsidiary detail: Express: Rs 1,832 Cr revenue (Q4), +46% YoY, 306 Mn volumes; PTL: Rs 622 Cr revenue (Q4), +20% YoY, 2 Mn metric tons (FY26); Transport Combined: Rs 2,453 Cr (Q4), 7.9% adj. EBITDA margin; SCS: Rs 729 Cr (FY26), margin pivoted from 2.2% to 10.9% service EBITDA.
growth verticals / optionality: New verticals funded by core cash flows: Local delivery, Cross-border logistics, Rapid (quick commerce enablement), and Financial services; Tech moat via Delhivery Labs deploying LLMs, AGVs, and automation to reduce unit costs and labor dependency.
margins & cost dynamics: Fuel price hikes (~Rs 3/liter) being passed through via indexed contracts (DPH clauses) and air surcharges; Q4 margins expanded despite fuel headwinds due to network productivity gains; Labor cost inflation mitigated by automation (AGVs, robotics) and AI-driven claims/documentation efficiency.
capex / expansion: FY26 Capex intensity at 4.7% of revenue (down from 7.8% in FY23); Targeting ~4% run-rate; Investments focused on mega-gateway automation (AGVs, sorters) and tech stack; No material increase expected from AI inference or robotics scaling.
capital allocation: Disciplined organic investment in tech/automation and new verticals; Strong balance sheet (Rs 4,500 Cr cash) enables potential inorganic opportunities; Focus on ROIC expansion (now 16%) and sustaining free cash flow generation.
risks & watch-items: Fuel price volatility impacting consumption; Regulatory changes on gig-worker wages; Competitive intensity from marketplace 1P logistics (though management views 3P as structurally cheaper); Execution risk in scaling new verticals (cross-border/financial).
management quality / tone: Confident and disciplined; Emphasis on 'profitable growth' and 'capital efficiency'; Celebratory of hitting FCF positive early; Pragmatic on competition (dismisses Amazon 3PL threat as 'old news'); Forward-looking on automation to counter labor tightness.
non-obvious takeaways: Management explicitly states that 1P logistics is structurally more expensive than 3P even after margins, suggesting a long-term structural shift of volume back to 3P as marketplaces face regulatory/labor cost pressures; The 'Delhivery Direct' app is quietly capturing significant SME/D2C share outside of aggregator channels; FCF positivity achieved despite full-year Ecom Express integration costs.
challenges → beneficiaries & losers:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rising fuel costs and labor wages squeezing logistics margins industry-wide | Delhivery Limited | beneficiary | High | Superior pass-through mechanisms (indexed contracts) and AI-driven cost reductions allow Delhivery to protect margins better than smaller peers; FCF inflection de-risks the equity story. |
| Marketplaces (Amazon/Flipkart) facing higher 1P logistics costs due to new gig-worker laws and minimum wage hikes | Delhivery Limited | beneficiary | Med | Structural cost disadvantage of 1P networks vs 3P will likely force marketplaces to shift more volume to third-party providers like Delhivery to optimize P&L. |
| Smaller 3PL players lacking capital for automation and tech moats face margin compression | Unorganized Logistics Players | loser | Med | Delhivery's scale and Rs 4,500 Cr cash pile allow aggressive investment in AGVs/AI that smaller players cannot match, widening the cost gap. |

themes.title: Logistics, ports & supply-chain formalization
themes.need: E-commerce, quick-commerce and GST-driven warehousing consolidation plus a 1P->3P shift drive an integrated-logistics up-cycle. DELHIVERY hit early FCF (>1B parcels, Express +46% rev) with Express targeting 16-18% margin; CONCOR/GATEWAY/JSWINFRA on rail/ports; ALLCARGO/MAHLOG/TVSSCS/VRLLOG on 3PL/road; BLUEDART/TCIEXP/WCIL/SNOWMAN on express + cold-chain; DELHIVERY/SHADOWFAX on quick-commerce fulfilment. Q1FY27's clearest turnaround datapoint: MAHLOG swung to a +INR 25.4cr PAT from a -INR 10.8cr loss on +23% revenue, with B2B Express (Rivigo) gross margin turning +6% from -3.8% and its EBITDA loss cut to -INR 1.6cr from -INR 11.8cr, guided to EBITDA breakeven within FY27, while Contract Logistics grew 26% with margin diluted only ~46bps on new-site start-up costs (opening a site almost every week).
themes.driver: Express/quick-commerce volume momentum; warehousing leasing; port/rail throughput; operating-leverage inflection.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Delhivery runs a pan-India integrated logistics network spanning Express Parcel, Part Truckload, Supply Chain Services, Full Truckload, International and Local services, offering door-to-door parcel delivery, B2B freight, warehousing and fulfilment, cross-border shipping, intracity delivery and supply-chain software. Its customers are e-commerce marketplaces, direct-to-consumer brands, SMEs, consumer-to-consumer senders and enterprise shippers across FMCG, consumer durables, consumer electronics, lifestyle, retail, automotive and manufacturing, with value-added services such as forward and reverse logistics, cash-on-delivery management, payment collection and fraud detection. The model is asset-light: Delhivery invests in critical service elements, automation and IP-sensitive parts of the network while delivering much of the physical capacity through network partners and last-mile partner agents, all orchestrated by a self-developed logistics operating system.

- Ecom Express Limited — subsidiary: Became a subsidiary on July 18, 2025; Delhivery completed acquisition of 99.87% on July 23, 2025 and of the remaining stake on December 10, 2025, making it a wholly-owned subsidiary from that date; CCI approval received June 17, 2025

- Delhivery Logistics (Shenzhen) Company Limited — subsidiary: Step-down subsidiary statutorily incorporated in FY23; no fund infusion made and non-operative as on date
- Delhivery UK Limited — subsidiary: Step-down subsidiary incorporated on January 15, 2026; yet to commence operations with no fund infusion made
- Falcon Autotech Private Limited — associate: Associate since January 04, 2022; 40.92% holding on a non-diluted basis and 39.33% on a diluted basis, with significant influence by way of shareholding; its share of profit is consolidated. As on March 31, 2026 the company had no joint venture under section 129(3)
- Delhivery Limited Gratuity Fund — related party: Post-employment benefit plan for the benefit of employees, disclosed as a related party under Ind AS 24

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body: Express: Rs 1,832 Cr revenue (Q4), +46% YoY, 306 Mn volumes; PTL: Rs 622 Cr revenue (Q4), +20% YoY, 2 Mn metric tons (FY26); Transport Combined: Rs 2,453 Cr (Q4), 7.9% adj. EBITDA margin; SCS: Rs 729 Cr (FY26), margin pivoted from 2.2% to 10.9% service EBITDA.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Express Parcel:** Door-to-door parcel delivery across India, Forward and reverse logistics, Cash-on-delivery management, Nationwide fulfillment
- **Part Truckload:** Express B2B part-truckload freight, Appointment-based deliveries, Freight on Delivery (FOD), Freight on Pickup (FOP), Electronic Proof of Delivery (e-POD)
- **Supply Chain Services:** Integrated warehousing (fulfilment) and transportation, Multi-tenant and dedicated Fulfilment Centres
- **Full Truckload:** Point-to-point and multi-point FTL services, Orion (asset-light freight exchange), Freight Index One (FTL pricing intelligence platform)
- **International:** International parcel shipping, Freight forwarding, Customs clearance and shipment visibility, Air-parcel service for SME and enterprise exports
- **Local:** Delhivery Local (on-demand intracity logistics), Delhivery Rapid (2-4 hour intra-city fulfilment)
- **Software:** Supply chain software / logistics software as a service

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: SCS business turned profitable with Rs 79 Cr service EBITDA (4x YoY); 2 new mandates signed/activated in Q4; Pipeline described as 'healthy' and focused on consumer durables, auto, and lifestyle sectors with disciplined client selection.

guidance.title: Guidance
guidance.body: Revenue Growth: Express volume grew 72-73% YoY in Q4; Margin: Express targeting 16-18% normative range, PTL margins expanding sequentially; Order Inflow: SCS pipeline margin-accretive with strict hurdle rates; Capex: Intensity reduced to 4.7% of revenue, targeting ~4% going forward, unaffected by AI/robotics pilots.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body: New verticals funded by core cash flows: Local delivery, Cross-border logistics, Rapid (quick commerce enablement), and Financial services; Tech moat via Delhivery Labs deploying LLMs, AGVs, and automation to reduce unit costs and labor dependency.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Formalisation of India's logistics market: customers are consolidating supply-chain spend with integrated 3PLs that offer reliability, visibility and nationwide reach, which management says drove share gains across all service lines in FY26
- Operating leverage compounding at scale — rising volumes plus a steadily improving cost structure from years of automation and network engineering investment, and added volume density post the Ecom Express integration; EBITDA margin moved from 1.6% in FY24 to 4.2% in FY25 to 6.1% in FY26
- India macro: IMF puts India as the fastest-growing large economy with growth around 6.5% in 2025 and 2026, nominal GDP of Rs 351 trillion (US$4.1 trillion) in FY2026, inflation around 4.7% in 2026, and consumption-led growth with PFCE rising as a share of GDP
- Market size and mix: total India logistics market of US$247-270 billion in FY25, with road transportation holding around 66% of cargo movement by tonnage; global logistics market growing at a 10.7% CAGR to US$18.23 trillion by 2030
- Rising consumer incomes — GNI per capita compounding ~9.3% between FY2020-2025, high- and middle-income households up from ~174 million in FY2020 to ~218 million in FY2025 with ~55 Mn more projected by FY2030
- Digital adoption: online shoppers projected to grow 8-10% CAGR from FY2025 to 365-430 million by FY2030, aided by cheap smartphones and among the lowest data costs globally
- New B2C commerce models — social commerce, omnichannel, quick commerce and D2C — plus category expansion into consumer durables, home and furniture, increasing demand for reliable organised logistics
- Evolving B2B models (direct-to-retail, direct-to-consumer) and government programmes like Make in India and PLI, driving demand for speed, precision and visibility in B2B supply chains
- Post-GST demand for integrated warehousing, transportation and technology from a single provider rather than mono-line players, plus growth of Tier 2 and beyond favouring players with deep national capabilities
- Technology-led transformation of the industry — automated sortation, AMRs, ASRS, wider WMS penetration, connected logistics/IoT and 5G, and AI in supply chain operations for large nationwide networks
- Headwind acknowledged by management: a challenging macro backdrop at the end of FY26 from geopolitical tensions affecting crude oil prices, with FY27 starting with significant geopolitical risk

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Fuel price hikes (~Rs 3/liter) being passed through via indexed contracts (DPH clauses) and air surcharges; Q4 margins expanded despite fuel headwinds due to network productivity gains; Labor cost inflation mitigated by automation (AGVs, robotics) and AI-driven claims/documentation efficiency.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Disciplined organic investment in tech/automation and new verticals; Strong balance sheet (Rs 4,500 Cr cash) enables potential inorganic opportunities; Focus on ROIC expansion (now 16%) and sustaining free cash flow generation.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Delhivery's capital expenditure is directed at fit-out infrastructure, state-of-the-art automation and IT assets, and tractor-trailers; automation covers parcel sorter systems, bag sortation systems and conveyance systems plus future-ready technologies such as automatic guided vehicles, automatic storage and retrieval systems and unmanned aerial vehicles. The company owns no real estate and only a portion of the fleet deployed in its network, so spend is deliberately concentrated on critical service elements and IP-sensitive parts of the network while physical capacity is delivered through partners. During FY26 it capitalised Rs 4,933.26 million of property, plant and equipment and intangible assets (excluding additions through acquisition and disposals), carried Rs 9.67 million of capital work in progress at year end, and funded the programme entirely through internal accruals and available cash; capex intensity fell from 5.2% of revenue in FY25 to 4.7% in FY26. The named FY26 projects were the expansion of mid-mile facilities in Chandigarh, Gurgaon, Ludhiana, Patna, Jaipur, Ahmedabad, Guwahati, Pune, Cochin, Lucknow, Goa, Purnia and Rudrapur, and the deployment of 123 additional 46ft tractors to raise the share of tractor-trailer capacity in the linehaul network. Automated material handling systems run at the Bhiwandi (Maharashtra), Tauru (Haryana) and Bengaluru (Karnataka) gateways, leaving 47 fully and semi-automated sortation centres, 129 gateways, 158 processing centres, 99 fulfilment centres (7.5 Mn sq ft of warehousing under management) and 4,848 last-mile distribution centres at 31 March 2026. On the inorganic side, Delhivery acquired 100.0% of Ecom Express, the #3 independent express player in India, for a consideration of about Rs 1,371 crore, aimed at cementing its position as the No. 1 independent express parcel player; one-time integration costs covered shutdown of redundant facilities, dismantling and transfer of automation equipment, exit from contracts and employee exits. Fleet and energy investment continued: 123 tractors added taking the tractor fleet to 624, 30 more LNG tractors taking that fleet to 50, over 3,000 contracted CNG- or electricity-powered vehicles in first-mile, carting and last-mile operations, and installed solar capacity of 5 MW at the end of FY26 which the company aims to augment during FY27. Liquidity to fund further organic and inorganic growth stood at Rs 45,553.32 million of cash and treasury investments against outstanding borrowings of Rs 25.35 million, with capital commitments (net of advances) of Rs 1,373.86 million contracted at 31 March 2026.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and disciplined; Emphasis on 'profitable growth' and 'capital efficiency'; Celebratory of hitting FCF positive early; Pragmatic on competition (dismisses Amazon 3PL threat as 'old news'); Forward-looking on automation to counter labor tightness.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Integrated single network: Express Parcel and Part Truckload run on the same gateways, line-haul and sortation infrastructure, letting capacity be shared across business lines and giving PTL shippers e-commerce-like turnaround times on several lanes
- Proprietary in-house logistics operating system with over 80 applications, plus configurable APIs and libraries that internal and external developers build on
- Data intelligence and machine learning across geo-location, network design, route optimisation, load aggregation, ETA prediction, product identification and fraud detection, drawing on fifteen years of proprietary shipment and telemetry data
- Automation scale: 47 fully and semi-automated sortation centres, 129 gateways and 10.4 million shipments/day rated automated sort capacity, with machine-vision guided truck loading and system-directed floor operations
- Network reach and density: services in 18,830 PIN codes covering approximately 97% of India's deliverable addresses, 71,362 partner agents and 52K+ active customers
- Asset-light model with no real-estate ownership and only part of the deployed fleet owned, using managed marketplaces to match partner capacity to demand — lower fixed cost and flexibility to seasonal swings
- Scale leadership: largest third-party Express Parcel network by volume and second-largest player in Express PTL, reinforced by the Ecom Express integration which added density, route viability and lower marginal cost per incremental parcel
- Experienced entrepreneurial team drawn from engineering, technology, operations, R&D and design across industries

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Fuel price volatility impacting consumption; Regulatory changes on gig-worker wages; Competitive intensity from marketplace 1P logistics (though management views 3P as structurally cheaper); Execution risk in scaling new verticals (cross-border/financial).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management explicitly states that 1P logistics is structurally more expensive than 3P even after margins, suggesting a long-term structural shift of volume back to 3P as marketplaces face regulatory/labor cost pressures; The 'Delhivery Direct' app is quietly capturing significant SME/D2C share outside of aggregator channels; FCF positivity achieved despite full-year Ecom Express integration costs.

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers
challenges.body:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rising fuel costs and labor wages squeezing logistics margins industry-wide | Delhivery Limited | beneficiary | High | Superior pass-through mechanisms (indexed contracts) and AI-driven cost reductions allow Delhivery to protect margins better than smaller peers; FCF inflection de-risks the equity story. |
| Marketplaces (Amazon/Flipkart) facing higher 1P logistics costs due to new gig-worker laws and minimum wage hikes | Delhivery Limited | beneficiary | Med | Structural cost disadvantage of 1P networks vs 3P will likely force marketplaces to shift more volume to third-party providers like Delhivery to optimize P&L. |
| Smaller 3PL players lacking capital for automation and tech moats face margin compression | Unorganized Logistics Players | loser | Med | Delhivery's scale and Rs 4,500 Cr cash pile allow aggressive investment in AGVs/AI that smaller players cannot match, widening the cost gap. |

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Ecom Express] The deck repeatedly carves out integration costs of the acquired Ecom Express business, quantified as ₹90 Cr for Q2FY26, ₹35 Cr for Q3FY26, ₹22 Cr for Q4FY26, ₹17 Cr for Q1FY27 and ₹148 Cr for FY26, described as net temporary costs pertaining to infrastructure, people, overheads, and business to be discontinued.
- [Ecom Express] Revenue from services in the service-line profitability table is stated to exclude revenue from Local, Rapid and Financial services, and Ecom Express businesses being transitioned — signalling that part of the acquired book is being wound down rather than retained.
- [Restatement basis] The quarterly income statement presents 'mgt. est.' columns for Q4FY26 and Q1FY27 that exclude the impact of Ecom Express related integration cost, so two different sets of figures for the same quarter appear in the deck (e.g. Q4FY26 revenue from services of ₹2,850 Cr reported versus ₹2,848 Cr on a management-estimate basis).
- [One-time items] Supply Chain Services FY25 adjusted EBITDA of ₹(64) Cr is attributed to a one-time impact of provisions on account of contractual matters, and Q2FY25 includes a reversal of ₹21 Cr of vendor advance provisions on account of settlement in our favour.
- [Associate] The income statement carries a separate 'share of profit / (loss) of associate (net)' line — ₹(3) Cr in Q1FY27, ₹9 Cr in Q4FY26 and ₹(8) Cr in Q1FY26 — but the deck does not name the associate.
